articles.title: Raipur man buys Rs 1 crore insurance policy, dies of cardiac arrest 15 months later, insurer refuses wife's claim over other policies, consumer commission orders Rs 1 crore payout with Rs 1.15 lakh compensation
articles.summary: RAIPUR: Holding an insurance company guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission,
articles.body: RAIPUR: Holding an insurance company guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Additional Bench, Raipur, has directed the insurer to pay a death insurance claim of Rs 1 crore to a woman whose husband died of cardiac arrest in Dec, 2019.The commission held that the insurance company's failure to honour the death claim, despite the policy being in force and the death having occurred during its validity, amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.The commission, comprising president Prashant Kundu and member Dr Anand Vergese, passed the order on Nov 3, while allowing a complaint filed by Chanda Pincha against insurance company.Apart from the Rs 1 crore insurance amount, the commission directed the company to pay Rs 1 lakh as compensation for mental and physical agony suffered by the complainant and Rs 15,000 towards litigation expenses.The entire amount has to be paid within forty-five days. In case of failure to comply with the order within the stipulated period, the insurer will also have to pay interest at 7% per annum until payment.According to the complaint, Chanda's husband, Pawan Pincha, a director of a private company, had purchased a policy, bearing number 007644841, on Sept 10, 2018. The policy provided a death cover of Rs 1 crore for the primary insured, Pawan, while his wife was the secondary insured with a cover of Rs 50 lakh.The policy had a tenure of 39 years, with maturity scheduled for Sept 10, 2057. The complainant's husband had paid a premium of Rs 36,969.40.Pawan died of a sudden cardiac arrest on Dec 21, 2019. Following his death, his wife, being the nominee, submitted a claim for the assured amount of Rs 1 crore. However, the insurance company rejected the claim on March 17, 2020, alleging that the deceased had failed to disclose several other life insurance policies taken from different insurance companies.The insurer maintained that the deceased had obtained multiple life insurance policies, including policies with substantial sums assured, without disclosing the relevant details in the proposal form. It argued that the suppression of material information amounted to a violation of the insurance contract and justified repudiation of the claim.The company also challenged the maintainability of the complaint, contending that the commission lacked territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction. It further alleged that the complainant had not impleaded the concerned insurance agent as a party to the proceedings.However, the commission, after examining the complaint, affidavits, insurance documents, medical records and correspondence between the parties, rejected the insurer's objections.The commission observed that the insurer had issued the policy after receiving the proposal and premium, and had an opportunity to examine the deceased's existing insurance coverage before accepting the proposal.It noted that the deceased had held other life insurance policies, but the insurer had failed to establish that the complainant was responsible for any concealment or that the circumstances justified repudiating the death claim.The order also referred to the fact that claims under certain other insurance policies held by the deceased had been settled by the respective insurance companies, while the claim under the disputed policy was rejected.It consequently directed the company to release the Rs 1 crore death benefit to the complainant, along with compensation and litigation expenses, within 45 days.Key highlightsWoman's husband buys a Rs 1 crore life insurance policy in September 2018 but dies of cardiac arrest in December 2019.Insurer rejects wife's death claim, alleging the deceased had failed to disclose multiple other life insurance policies.Raipur consumer commission rejects the insurer's defence, observing that it had an opportunity to verify the deceased's existing insurance coverage before issuing the policy.Commission holds the insurer guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices, directing it to pay Rs 1 crore with Rs 1 lakh compensation and Rs 15,000 litigation expenses.Insurer directed to make the payment within 45 articles.title: Jovem brasileiro morto a facada na Inglaterra era apaixonado pelo país | G1
articles.standfirst: Tiago Henrique Barbosa Ferreira, de 23 anos, morreu enquanto trabalhava fazendo entregas em Stonehouse. Em entrevista, Taciana Ferreira afirmou que o irmão teve a vida interrompida por um crime horrível.
articles.summary: Em entrevista, Taciana Ferreira afirmou que o irmão teve a vida interrompida por um crime horrível.
articles.body:
Tiago Henrique Barbosa Ferreira, de 23 anos, morto a facadas enquanto trabalhava fazendo entregas em Stonehouse, na Inglaterra, era apaixonado pelo país, segundo a irmã, Taciana Ferreira. Em entrevista à TV Anhanguera, ela contou que o jovem viveu o sonho dele, mas teve a vida interrompida por um crime horrível.

"Ele era apaixonado por esse país, o Tiago era apaixonado por Londres. Eu pedia muito para ele vir embora, ficar aqui com a gente. Ele viveu o sonho dele, vivia a vida dele feliz e teve a vida interrompida por uma tragédia, um crime horrível", disse Taciana.

O crime aconteceu no domingo (15) e as autoridades locais divulgaram o caso nesta quinta-feira (19). Daryl John Ackland, de 46 anos, foi preso suspeito do crime . A reportagem não localizou sua defesa.

De acordo com a namorada de Tiago, Taciane Magalhães, o jovem era natural de Anápolis e morava no país havia cinco anos. Segundo ela, Tiago saiu de Wembley na manhã do crime para fazer entregas em Stonehouse, cidade vizinha. O jovem costumava manter contato de hora em hora e os dois chegaram a conversar por chamada de vídeo naquela mesma noite.

Tiago Henrique Barbosa Ferreira era natural de Goiás e foi morto durante um assalto — Foto: Divulgação/Gloucestershire Constabulary

Por volta das 23h, ela afirmou que não conseguiu mais contato com o namorado. Segundo informaram as autoridades locais aos familiares, foi nesse momento que um homem teria abordado Tiago com uma faca para roubar o carro dele. Taciane acredita que o companheiro possa ter reagido ao assalto antes de ser atingido no peito por um golpe de faca.

"Provavelmente ele reagiu porque ele dizia que reagiria a um assalto, sabe? Durante as nossas conversas do dia a dia", disse Taciane.

Segundo informações divulgadas pela polícia local, Tiago chegou a ser encontrado inconsciente na rua com uma perfuração. Ele chegou a ser socorrido pelo serviço de emergência, mas não resistiu aos ferimentos e morreu no local, informaram as autoridades. A família de Thiago tenta trazer o corpo dele para Anápolis.

Taciane contou, ainda, que após o crime os policiais informaram que o suspeito fugiu com o carro da vítima e chegou a tentar invadir uma casa e agredir duas pessoas antes de ser preso. De acordo com a polícia de Gloucestershire, Daryl John Ackland, de 46 anos, deve ser julgado ainda nesta quinta-feira (19) pelos crimes:

Assassinato de Tiago Henrique Barbosa Ferreira;

Agravante de pegar veículo sem consentimento;

Dirigir em desacordo com as condições da habilitação;

Taciane, que é do Rio de Janeiro, destacou que pretende deixar o país após o ocorrido, mas ainda não conseguiu dinheiro suficiente para voltar ao Brasil, segundo ela.

articles.title: Ronaldo Machado Salles: ex-vereador morre em temporal em Tupanciretã | G1
articles.standfirst: Chuva durante a madrugada destruiu casas, deixou 60 feridos e interrompeu abastecimento de luz e água na cidade. PSDB lamentou a morte de Ronaldo Machado Salles.
articles.summary: Ronaldo Machado Salles foi vítima de um temporal com suspeita de microexplosão que destruiu casas e cortou serviços essenciais no interior do Rio Grande do Sul.
articles.body:
Ronaldo Machado Salles, ex-vereador de Tupanciretã , é um dos mortos na tempestade com vento e granizo que atingiu a cidade de 20 mil habitantes na Região Central do Rio Grande do Sul, na madrugada desta sexta-feira (20).

A informação foi confirmada pelo presidente estadual do PSDB, Moisés Barboza. Ronaldo foi eleito como vereador em Tupanciretã por sete mandatos: em 2020, 2016, 2012, 2008, 2004, 2000 e 1992.

Em nota, Barboza lamentou a morte ( veja íntegra abaixo ). "Ronaldo dedicou parte de sua trajetória à vida pública e ao trabalho em favor da comunidade de Tupanciretã, deixando sua contribuição à história política do município e do nosso partido", disse.

Além de Ronaldo, morreu uma pessoa ainda não identificada e Hortência Bueno Alves, 85 anos .

Segundo dados da Defesa Civil, foram 60 feridos e mais de 5 mil casas danificadas na cidade .

O Centro de Monitoramento da Defesa Civil do RS analisou imagens e vídeos da tempestade que atingiu Tupanciretã na madrugada desta sexta-feira. Há indícios de que a cidade tenha sido atingida por uma microexplosão . Uma estação do Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) registrou rajadas de vento de 114 km/h durante o temporal.

"Até o momento, não é possível confirmar a ocorrência de um tornado no município. As evidências apontam para ventos severos associados à supercélula, possivelmente provocados por uma microexplosão. A possibilidade de tornado não está completamente descartada, mas o fenômeno, isoladamente, não explicaria a extensão dos danos registrados na cidade", destaca a Defesa Civil.

Os dados do radar meteorológico de Porto Alegre indicam a atuação da supercélula por volta das 3h19.

A Defesa Civil do RS emitiu, às 2h38, um alerta vermelho por SMS para a região, incluindo Tupanciretã, indicando risco de granizo grande e vendaval, com risco muito alto de destelhamentos. O alerta teve vigência até as 3h37.

" O PSDB do Rio Grande do Sul lamenta profundamente o falecimento de nosso ex-vereador e ex-presidente da Câmara Municipal de Tupanciretã, Ronaldo Machado Salles, uma das vítimas já confirmadas da tempestade que devastou o município na madrugada desta sexta-feira (20).

Ronaldo dedicou parte de sua trajetória à vida pública e ao trabalho em favor da comunidade de Tupanciretã, deixando sua contribuição à história política do município e do nosso partido.

Neste momento de profunda tristeza, manifestamos nossa solidariedade aos familiares, amigos e a toda a comunidade de Tupanciretã, que enfrenta dias de dor e perdas em decorrência dessa tragédia.

Presidente estadual PSDB do Rio Grande do Sul"

articles.title: Execução no Texas: Condenado grita de dor em processo de uma hora | G1
articles.standfirst: Reinaldo Dennes, de 70 anos, recebeu injeção de pentobarbital, droga que atua no sistema nervoso central. Execução deveria durar apenas alguns minutos.
articles.summary: A execução no Texas de Reinaldo Dennes durou uma hora e foi marcada por gritos de dor do condenado após aplicação da injeção letal de pentobarbital.
articles.body:
Reinaldo Dennes (de camisa branca), de 70 anos, foi condenado à morte pelo assassinato de um vendedor de diamantes em 1996 — Foto: Houston Chronicle via Getty Images

Um homem condenado à morte gritou, aparentemente de dor, durante sua execução, que durou uma hora, no estado do Texas, nos Estados Unidos.

"Não está funcionando como deveria", exclamou Reinaldo Dennes, de 70 anos, enquanto recebia uma injeção de pentobarbital, droga que atua no sistema nervoso central, de acordo com testemunhas. Normalmente, esse tipo de execução dura apenas alguns minutos.

Um porta-voz do Departamento de Justiça Criminal do Texas admitiu que houve tentativas frustradas de encontrar as veias de Dennes para aplicar a injeção, mas disse que ele reclamou de dores em partes do corpo que não tinham sido tocadas pelos agentes.

O caso de Dennes vem à tona semanas após o fracasso na execução de Christa Pike , que sobreviveu a duas doses letais de pentobarbital em setembro desse ano. Ela chegou a ficar internada em estado crítico, mas deixou o hospital no fim de outubro.

Pike é, provavelmente, a única pessoa a ter sobrevivido a uma tentativa de execução pelo método de injeção letal nos EUA.

Dennes foi sentenciado à morte pelo assassinato do vendedor de diamantes Janos Szucs, em 1996. Sua execução aconteceu no mesmo dia em que outro detento foi colocado no corredor da morte no estado da Flórida.

Michael Graczyk, repórter da agência Associated Press que testemunhou várias execuções ao longo da carreira, explicou que os condenados costumam esperar longos períodos até serem levados à câmara, tanto porque eles resistem ao procedimento como porque, em alguns casos, os agentes têm dificuldades em encontrar as veias.

No caso de Dennes, quando as testemunhas foram autorizadas a assistir ao processo, ele começou a gritar: "Que dor! Vão, vão!", conta Gracsyk. Depois, ainda disse um palavrão e clamou ao "pai" que o "livrasse da dor" para, então, reclamar de dores na perna direita. Antes de outro xingamento, ele ainda disse: "Não acho isso normal!"

Outra testemunha, o reverendo Jeff Hood, contou ao jornal norte-americano USA Today que a morte de Dennes foi a "pior, de longe, que ele já tinha visto".

"Ele [Dennes[ gritava: 'Minha perna, minha perna, minha perna'", disse. "Daí falou: 'Não está funcionando como deveria'".

O uso do pentobarbital, um barbitúrico de ação curta, voltou a ser criticado desde o caso de Pike, de 50 anos, em setembro. O fracasso nas duas tentativas de executá-la chocou o mundo. Desde que teve alta, ela voltou à prisão, onde está há três décadas pelo assassinato de Colleen Slemmer, em 1995.

Um potente sedativo que desacelera o organismo, incluindo o sistema nervoso, o pentobarbital também é utilizado no tratamento de certas doenças. Em altas doses, se transforma em uma injeção letal que leva à morte.

Seu uso para esse fim foi revisto no ano passado, após uma análise que havia começado ainda no governo de Joe Biden (2021-2024) apontar preocupações sobre o quanto a droga pode causar "dor e sofrimento desnecessários".

Biden, inclusive, proibiu o uso do pentobarbital em execuções federais. Ele segue sendo utilizado em alguns estados porque, pela lei dos EUA, eles podem escolher seus próprios métodos de execução.

articles.title: Jason Statham swapped Hollywood and Los Angeles for a quieter family life in the English countryside; his partner Rosie says their children now enjoy the same farm experiences she had growing up
articles.summary: From Los Angeles to Britain and now towards a quieter countryside life, the couple’s parenting priorities reflect a desire to give their children
articles.body: From Los Angeles to Britain and now towards a quieter countryside life, the couple’s parenting priorities reflect a desire to give their children something fame cannot buy: freedom, family connections and the simple joys of growing up outdoors. Hollywood often promises glamour, luxury homes and a life surrounded by attention. But for Jason Statham and his partner, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, a different kind of luxury appears to matter more when it comes to raising their children.The couple have been steadily moving towards a quieter family life in England, away from the hustle of Los Angeles and the constant attention that can accompany celebrity. Their decision is not simply about changing homes. It is about choosing the kind of childhood they want their children to remember. For Rosie, that childhood involves open spaces, farm life, nature and the freedom to explore. And she wants her children to experience the same.Trading city life for a childhood closer to natureRosie and Jason moved from Los Angeles to London in 2020, partly to create a more stable family environment and make it easier for Jason to work closer to home. The move also meant that their children could grow up in Britain, surrounded by family and a familiar support system. In interviews, Rosie has spoken about how important education, family connections and a sense of belonging are to their decision. Jason's parents live nearby and are actively involved in the children's lives, allowing the family to enjoy a support system that can be difficult to maintain when constantly travelling.But London was not necessarily the final destination. Rosie has spoken about wanting a slower lifestyle, one where weekends are not filled with rushing between activities and where children can simply enjoy being outdoors. Her vision of countryside living is less about luxury and more about space, freedom and a childhood that feels uncomplicated. For parents everywhere, that desire is familiar: creating an environment where children can feel rooted rather than constantly occupied.The farm memories Rosie wants to pass onRosie grew up on a farm in Devon, England, where her childhood was shaped by animals, outdoor adventures and a relatively simple way of life. Now, she wants her children, Jack and Isabella, to experience that same sense of freedom. In an interview with The Sunday Times in 2025, she shared that during summers in Devon, the children get to run around on a farm just as she did growing up. She described the experience as particularly special.That detail says a lot about her approach to parenting. Rather than trying to recreate her childhood exactly, she is giving her children opportunities to connect with the outdoors, explore their surroundings and build memories away from screens and schedules.Running around on a farm, collecting sticks, observing animals, getting muddy or simply spending an afternoon outside may seem ordinary. Yet these experiences can give children opportunities to develop curiosity, confidence, independence and an appreciation of nature. For Rosie, passing on these experiences appears to be less about creating a perfect childhood and more about allowing her children to enjoy the kind of everyday adventures that stay with them long after they grow up.Why a quieter home matters to their parenting choicesThe couple's move away from Los Angeles was also influenced by the practical realities of raising children while working in the entertainment industry. Jason's filming schedules could mean spending long stretches away from home. Rosie has explained that moving to London made it easier for him to work and return home at the end of the day, giving the family more time together. She has described Jason as a hands-on father who enjoys playing with the children, carrying them around and being actively involved in their everyday lives.The couple have also made deliberate choices to protect their children's privacy. They have largely avoided sharing their children's faces publicly and have kept them away from the red-carpet spotlight. Their decisions reflect a parenting priority that many families can relate to, regardless of their circumstances: children need time, attention, stability and room to grow without feeling that every part of their lives has to be seen by others.A reminder that childhood does not need to be extravagantThe Statham family’s lifestyle may be far removed from that of most parents, but the values behind their choices are surprisingly relatable. A peaceful environment, time spent with family, outdoor play and the freedom to explore are things many parents wish they could give their children. Childhood memories are often built around the simplest moments: helping feed animals, running through fields, climbing trees, spending time with grandparents or discovering something new without being hurried.Rosie's wish to recreate those farm experiences for Jack and Isabella highlights an important parenting lesson. Children do not necessarily need every experience to be organised, expensive or extraordinary. Sometimes, what they need most is the freedom to be children.And perhaps that is what Jason and Rosie are seeking as they move towards a quieter life. Beyond movie premieres, fame and busy schedules, they want their children to have a childhood filled with laughter, family traditions, muddy shoes and memories of being outdoors. In a world where childhood is increasingly structured around screens, classes and schedules, their choice offers a gentle reminder to parents: giving children time and space to explore may be one of the most meaningful gifts we can offer.You use AI every day. articles.title: Donald Trump urged senators to back an energy bill he said would lower electricity costs; the US Senate has now passed it 62-33, requiring large AI data centres to pay more of their grid-upgrade costs
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming industries and fueling demand for computing power and the infrastructure that powers the technology is under
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is transforming industries and fueling demand for computing power and the infrastructure that powers the technology is under mounting pressure. The growth of data centers and electricity use in the US is prompting concerns about household utility bills and the country's ability to generate and distribute sufficient power. In this context, US lawmakers passed a major bipartisan energy bill that aims to accelerate infrastructure development, while placing greater responsibility on large AI data centers to fund the expansion of the electricity grid.Senate passes major energy permitting billAccording to Associated Press and Reuters, the U.S. Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.The legislation is designed to accelerate the approval process for major energy infrastructure projects, including power plants, transmission lines, pipelines and other facilities needed to increase electricity supplies. It now moves to the Republican-controlled House of Representatives, which must approve the measure before it can go to President Donald Trump.The bill has been in the works for about four years, and its passage is one of Congress's biggest efforts in years to address delays affecting big energy projects, Reuters reported.The proposal also comes amid growing worries about the electricity demand of artificial intelligence, especially the expansion of huge data centers that use a lot of power.Trump supports bill to slash electricity pricesPresident Donald Trump had pushed senators to vote for the measure, which he described as a critical step toward boosting American energy independence and reducing household costs.Trump called it a big win for U.S. energy production, saying that faster approvals would help the country build pipelines, mines and power plants without lengthy regulatory delays, the Associated Press reported.The bill had the support of 15 Democrats, among them Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, and most Republican senators. But it faced opposition from Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Josh Hawley of Missouri.The deal was negotiated by four lawmakers including Republican Senators Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee and Democratic Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse. Capito welcomed the Senate’s passage, calling it a key step toward addressing affordability concerns, Reuters reported.AI data centers must shoulder more of grid costsOne of the most important provisions concerns the financial liability of large artificial intelligence data centers.The legislation would require those facilities to pay a bigger share of the electricity grid upgrades tied to their power needs, Reuters reported.The provision comes as the debate grows over whether average electricity users should pay for the expansion of infrastructure needed by energy-hungry tech firms. As AI adoption accelerates, data centers will need ever more reliable electricity supplies. Expanding their capacity can be expensive, requiring new transmission lines and upgrades to existing grid systems.The legislation is intended to ease concerns about how the costs of energy infrastructure are shared by forcing big data center operators to contribute more to the upgrade.Environment concerns raised faster approvalsThe proposal has drawn criticism from environmental organizations and some Democratic lawmakers despite bipartisan support. The legislation would tighten deadlines for federal environmental reviews and change some provisions of existing laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act, the Associated Press reported.Supporters say the current approval process can delay infrastructure projects for years, adding to construction costs and delaying electricity supplies to consumers.But environmental groups worry that less regulatory oversight could spur fossil fuel development, while diluting protections for communities, wildlife and natural resources.Critics also have raised concerns about the legislation’s impact on tribal sovereignty and consultation with Indigenous communities, according to Reuters.Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., opposed the measure, saying tribal rights and environmental consequences need to be studied in more detail before Congress approves the changes.Bill moves to House in larger energy debateThe bill was not passed without procedural wrangling. Senate Republicans blocked attempts by lawmakers to change the bill, so several proposed changes didn’t make the final version, The Associated Press reported.Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell also criticized the pace of the legislative process, raising concerns about protections for tribal communities, waterways and wildlife. Still, supporters say the United States needs a more streamlined process for approving infrastructure projects to keep electricity supplies in step with rising demand.The proposal will now go to the House of Representatives for further consideration. Trump has said he would sign the bill if it were to pass Congress.The bill is a big step toward balancing energy affordability, infrastructure development, and the rising costs of powering America's digital economy because electricity use is rising and AI infrastructure is being built out at a rapid pace.Images Courtesy: istock and InstagramYou use AI every day. articles.title: After more than 10 years as a secretary, Bette Nesmith Graham made correction fluid in her kitchen; by 1964, Liquid Paper was selling over 5,000 bottles a week
articles.summary: Discover how Bette Nesmith Graham transformed her passion for art and determination into a revolutionary business with Liquid Paper, changing the office supply industry forever.
articles.body: Parenting is never easy, and every parent goes to great lengths to provide for their children. However, single parents face even bigger challenges as they shoulder the responsibilities of raising a family alone. As a single mother in the 1950s, Bette Nesmith Graham (formerly known as Bette Clair McMurray) struggled to support her son financially on her meager secretarial salary while navigating technical challenges that threatened her job. Through hard work and sheer determination, this high school dropout became a businesswoman and helped change the office supply industry.One day, Bette stood outside the Texas Bank and Trust, watching the artists paint the windows in different colors for the Christmas season. She paid close attention to how they worked, noticing how effortlessly they painted over misplaced brushstrokes. Ultimately, her love for the arts and perseverance saved her career.At the young age of 17, Bette dropped out of high school to attend secretarial school and marry her longtime sweetheart, Warren Nesmith. Her perseverance helped her raise her infant son, Michael, while Warren served abroad as a soldier during World War II. The pair divorced in 1946, leaving Bette as a single mother who could not afford to lose her job, as it was her main source of income.The transition from manual typewriters to electric typewritersBy the 1950s, the clatter of typewriters was everywhere. At that time, several offices switched from manual typewriters to electric ones. While the electric typewriters automated daily tasks and maximized productivity, their messy carbon-film ribbons and sensitive keys led to more typos. An eraser could fix this problem, but the carbon ink would smudge all over the page, requiring a new draft due to a single mistake.Throughout her decade-plus career, Bette had climbed the ranks to become the executive secretary to the chairman of the Texas Bank and Trust. Although she was an organized and capable secretary, her typing accuracy suffered once offices switched to electric typewriters. As a result, she made frequent slip-ups and searched for ways to fix them.Remembering the artists painting the bank windows, Bette brought a small jar of white, water-based tempera paint into the office one day and used a watercolor brush to erase the typos. It worked remarkably well. Bette used her liquid creation for a while before other secretaries noticed and eventually asked her to create bottles of the wonder fluid for them.Motivated by the positive feedback, Bette began filling orders at night from her North Dallas home for local secretaries. At the same time, she worked alongside her son’s chemistry teacher and an industrial polymer chemist to refine the formula, which she initially called Mistake Out. Bette wanted to ensure that her product was perfect before it entered the market.Despite the surging demand for her correction fluid, Bette couldn’t afford the $400 patent application fee in 1956, as she earned $300 per month as a secretary. She kept her day job, and at night, she contacted potential buyers and sent out samples of her newly renamed Liquid Paper correcting fluid from Dallas to San Antonio and Houston.From dropout to successful entrepreneurIn 1957, Bette pitched her product to IBM, though the company declined. Soon after, she hired a small team of employees and began selling Liquid Paper to area office supply stores. According to the USPTO, Bette landed her first major order the next year when Fortune 500 behemoth General Electric asked for 400 bottles in three colors. Shortly thereafter, Bette began getting orders from major corporations including IBM, which had previously turned her down.Despite a promising start, the company struggled to make profits in its early years. However, things took a turn for the better in 1962, when Bette married her second husband, Robert Graham, a former food salesman. She used her partner’s expertise to sell Liquid Paper to office supply stores across the country. As orders increased, the company’s operations went from Bette’s kitchen to her garage, then to her trailer, and ultimately to a four-room house. By 1964, Bette’s business was profitable and selling 5,000 bottles per week.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After years as a store clerk, J.C. Penney put $500 of his savings into a Wyoming store in 1902; by 1917, his Golden Rule chain had nearly 200 locations
articles.summary: Explore the inspiring journey of J.C. Penney, from a humble store clerk to the founder of a retail giant that once boasted over 2,000 locations nationwide.
articles.body: Once among the largest department store chains in the world, the J.C. Penney Company began in a one-room shop in a small Wyoming coal-mining town. The founder was James Cash Penney, a Missourian who was born in 1875, and he moved west after his doctor told him that the drier climate of the region would benefit his health.At first, James made a stop in Longmont, Colorado, where he opened a butcher shop in 1898. His venture relied on orders from a local hotel. When the principled James refused to give liquor to the hotel chef in exchange for the business, it eventually led to the venture being shut down.From clerk to business magnate As per the accounts shared by the WyoHistory organization, James started working as a store clerk at the local Golden Rule store, part of a small dry goods chain that sold fabric, sewing supplies, and work clothes. Thomas Callahan and Guy Johnson, the owners of the store, were impressed by James’ work ethic and salesmanship, and they asked him to manage their Evanston, Wyoming store in 1899.After three years, the owners offered him a one-third partnership in their new store in Kemmerer, Wyoming, which was located on the Oregon Short Line Railroad, a subsidiary of the Union Pacific. The town had boomed in no time after coal was struck in 1897 and had 1,000 residents by the time James got there. The railroad required coal, the coal mines needed miners, and the miners and their families desired dry goods.James invested $2,000 ($500 in savings and $1,500 borrowed) for his share of the store, an investment that turned out to be immensely profitable. The Golden Rule store sold exactly what the mining families needed, and it sold those goods at affordable prices. During its first year, which happened to be 1902, the store netted $8,000 on sales of more than $28,000. It also established the groundwork for a retail empire.Expansion of the J.C. Penney EmpireThen, James planned to expand, and he kicked off with Wyoming, where he opened stores in Cumberland and Rock Springs. In 1907, he made a smart business move by purchasing his partners’ Wyoming holdings, and he used them as a launching pad to open stores in Idaho and Utah and, ultimately, all over the nation. After two years, he moved the headquarters to Salt Lake City.In 1913, he changed the name of Golden Rule Stores to his own, marking the birth of the J. C. Penney Company. James’ business philosophy was simple: hire good employees, train them properly, and sell quality products at a small markup to keep prices down. His tactic worked. By 1917, the chain had rolled out nearly 200 outlets; by 1928, it had expanded to over 1,000. Eventually, the number surpassed 2,000 as the store found niches on Main Streets across America, though shifting retail trends later forced the company to downsize to roughly 1,100 locations.James began his career when cars were still rare on American streets and managed the company through world wars and the Great Depression before stepping down as chairman in 1958. Even after stepping back from running the company, Penney stayed closely connected to the business until his death at the age of 95 in 1971. Nearly two decades after his death, the company moved its headquarters from New York City to suburban Dallas.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After earning 50 cents a day as a bookkeeper, John D. Rockefeller used $1,000 in savings and a $1,000 loan to start a business in 1859; eleven years later, he co-founded Standard Oil
articles.summary: Explore the life of John D. Rockefeller, from his humble beginnings as a bookkeeper to co-founding Standard Oil and becoming a billionaire, amidst controversies and antitrust challenges.
articles.body: A career that started with ledger books would eventually place John D. Rockefeller at the heart of a legal tussle over monopoly power. His path between the two ran straight through Cleveland’s oil refining trade, which he entered at the cusp of the American oil industry's growth.Early ambition and the first refinery bet According to the Rockefeller Archive Center, Rockefeller was born on July 8, 1839, in Richford, New York, the second of six children of William A. and Eliza Davison Rockefeller. His family moved to Ohio in 1853. He attended Central High School in Cleveland, then left in 1855 to study at Folsom Mercantile College. He completed its six-month business course in just three months and joined Hewitt & Tuttle, a firm that dealt in commission sales and shipments. He initially started as an assistant bookkeeper there, earning 50 cents a day, and climbed up to the rank of cashier and head bookkeeper.In 1859, he entered into a partnership with Maurice B. Clark in the commission business, using $1,000 in savings and a $1,000 loan. This was the same year when the first oil well was drilled at Titusville, Pennsylvania. This discovery helped establish the petroleum industry. Cleveland subsequently became a refining centre, and Rockefeller and Clark entered the business in 1863. With Samuel Andrews, they built and operated an oil refinery named Andrews, Clark & Co., and simultaneously continued their commission work.Two years later, in 1865, there was, however, a disagreement over the management of their business, and they decided to sell the refinery to whichever partner offered the highest bid. The situation ended with Rockefeller buying it for $72,500. He then sold his other interests and joined Andrews in a new firm, Rockefeller & Andrews, the Rockefeller Archive Center noted.How Standard Oil cornered the refining market Against this backdrop, the oil trade was expanding as kerosene became more widely used for lighting. In 1870, along with his brother William, Andrews, Henry M. Flagler, Stephen V. Harkness and other partners, Rockefeller established the Standard Oil Company. The business centred on refining oil rather than sourcing or drilling oil wells.Rockefeller’s business acumen paid close attention to operating costs and the use of refinery by-products. Standard Oil brought more of its labour and supporting work, such as barrel-making and pipelines, in-house. It also invested in research for materials other refiners discarded or overlooked. After the company purchased an Ohio oil field that contained sour crude, it developed a process that removed impurities from oil.According to the Library of Congress, in the first three months of 1872, it bought 22 of the 26 refineries in Cleveland, which were either closed or on the cusp of bankruptcy. Standard Oil also secured favourable railway rates and promised large and regular shipments. The company had one edge over other refineries: it moved oil at a lower cost.The Rockefeller Archive Center records that in 1882, Standard Oil’s properties were brought together under the Standard Oil Trust. The trust had an initial capital of $70 million and 42 certificate holders, of which Rockefeller owned one-third of its certificates, the Archive Center noted. By the late 1880s, Standard Oil controlled 90% of American refineries.Antitrust backlash and a billion-dollar legacyBut the company’s market power and railway arrangements attracted political scrutiny. States and federal lawmakers adopted measures against monopolies and railway rebates. One such strong critic was journalist Ida Tarbell, who published a detailed criticism of Standard Oil’s business practices.In 1911, the US Supreme Court ruled that Standard Oil had violated the Sherman Antitrust Act and ordered the dissolution of Standard Oil, according to the Library of Congress. The separate units endured as independent businesses, and later some developed into major oil corporations, including ExxonMobil. Irrespective of the controversy, Rockefeller’s wealth continued to grow. Newspapers at the time had touted him as the world’s first billionaire in 1916, the Library of Congress noted.He had begun to give away part of his wealth decades earlier, and supported his church and other causes. His later philanthropic legacy included the University of Chicago, the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, the General Education Board and the Rockefeller Foundation established in 1913. The university achieved incorporation in 1890 after others pledged the balance of its $1 million endowment within 90 days of Rockefeller’s conditional offer of $600,000, the Rockefeller Archive Center noted. Rockefeller passed away on May 23, 1937. He was 97 when he died at his home in Ormond Beach, Florida.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ex-IAF vice-chief slams UK report claiming India has 32 Rafales instead of 36 as 'patently false'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A former Indian Air Force vice-chief has debunked a controversial report by a British aviation magazine that listed four fewer Rafale fighter
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A former Indian Air Force vice-chief has debunked a controversial report by a British aviation magazine that listed four fewer Rafale fighter jets in the IAF’s fleet, showing just 32 aircraft as compared to 36 India had acquired from France. Air Marshal Narmdeshwar Tiwari (retd), who played active roles during the Kargil war and Operation Sindoor in May last year, called FlightGlobal’s figures “patently false”.FlightGlobal’s latest World Air Forces directory report has neither given any explanation nor provided any evidence for the reduced number of Rafale jets with the IAF. Under the ‘India’ head, the report just showed the ‘active’ number of Rafale jets as 32 and showed 114 such 4.5-generation fighter jets under the category ‘ordered’ which India is planning to acquire from France after signing a formal contract. Even in its last year’s report, published months after Op Sindoor, FlightGlobal had listed 35 active Rafales, one aircraft fewer than the actual number.Air Marshal Tiwari (retd) questioned the credibility of the aviation magazine’s sources. “FlightGlobal should re-evaluate their sources. The same sources gave specific tail numbers, which since have been flying in various exercises including international ones. The same sources said that Sqn Ldr Shivangi Singh was taken as a prisoner of war (PoW). We all know how that turned out,” Air Marshal Tiwari, who retired last year in Dec after Op Sindoor, posted on X on Thursday night.Pakistani media outlets and pro-Pakistan social media handles had then said that Sqn Ldr Shivangi was held hostage as a PoW. After the conflict, a smiling Shivangi had posed with President Droupadi Murmu at Ambala airbase, debunking claims of her being held hostage by Pakistan as a PoW.In June this year, an IAF tender sought ‘bridge support’ (maintenance) for all 36 Rafale fighter jets, contradicting Pakistan’s repeated claims that India had lost several Rafale jets during Op Sindoor. Though Indian military leadership had repeatedly rubbished such claims, Pakistan kept insisting that it had downed several multi-role Rafale fighters during the conflict.Last year in June, Dassault Aviation CEO Éric Trappier called Pakistan’s claims of shooting down IAF’s Rafale jets “inaccurate”, while noting that Indian authorities had not communicated details of any Rafale losses.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Ohio families say 250 trees meant to shield their homes from coal-ash ponds were cut down during demolition of a power plant; a jury has now awarded the neighbours $1.65 million for the lost buffer
articles.summary: A US jury has awarded $1.65 million to a group of Ohio residents after hundreds of trees that formed a protective greenbelt around their homes were cut
articles.body: A US jury has awarded $1.65 million to a group of Ohio residents after hundreds of trees that formed a protective greenbelt around their homes were cut down during the demolition of a former coal-fired power plant.The residents of Pierce Township had sued Commercial Liability Partners (CLP), the company that bought the 1,443-acre site of the former William C. Beckjord power plant from Duke Energy in 2018. They alleged that the company violated an agreement to preserve the greenbelt, which was meant to separate nearby homes from coal-ash ponds along the Ohio River.According to WCPO, the jury announced its verdict on Wednesday after deliberating for around two-and-a-half hours. It awarded the residents $1,654,080 to compensate for the destruction of trees and fund restoration of the forest.The lawsuit was filed in 2019 by Neighbors Opposing Pit Expansion (NOPE), a local residents' group. The organisation had sought $3.3 million in damages, arguing that the loss of the trees had damaged the greenbelt and affected the surrounding environment.Residents said logging destroyed decades-old greenbeltResidents told the court that bulldozers and logging trucks had cut through the mature forest, removing around 250 trees, including pine, walnut, cherry and maple varieties. Some of the trees had grown as tall as 50 feet.They said the logging left deep tracks in the forest, destroyed vegetation and changed the character of the area. Residents also reported a decline in wildlife and birds, while invasive honeysuckle spread across parts of the land.Pierce Township Board of Trustees Chairman Allen Freeman said the tree line had been visibly cut down after CLP took ownership of the property in 2018.The residents argued that the greenbelt was protected under a 1986 agreement between the local community and the then-owner, Cincinnati Gas & Electric. The agreement required the preservation of the buffer as a “substantially undisturbed” area.They also said the trees and their root systems helped stabilise the hillsides around the coal-ash ponds, while shielding homes from the view of the waste-storage site.CLP disputed the residents' claims and questioned the amount of compensation they were seeking. Its lawyer argued that there were no photographs showing the condition of the greenbelt before the logging and described the $3.3 million demand as unreasonable.Jury awards money for tree replacement and forest restorationExperts presented competing estimates of the damage and the cost of restoring the greenbelt during the trial.A tree expert called by CLP suggested that the residents should receive no compensation for the large trees that had been cut down. He estimated that planting seedlings in the 17-acre greenbelt would cost around $25,000, arguing that the area was already recovering.However, an expert representing NOPE estimated that restoring the forest and removing invasive honeysuckle would cost approximately $500,000. He also valued the loss of the trees at around $2.7 million, saying the logging had damaged the forest's canopy and compacted the soil.The jury ultimately awarded $1,142,860 for replacing 233 trees, $102,000 to remove invasive species, $28,600 for revegetating the land and $160,620 for caring for the newly planted saplings.The Beckjord power plant, built in the 1950s, was shut down by Duke Energy in 2014. More than five million tons of coal ash were stored in unlined, man-made ponds at the site near the Ohio River.Coal ash is the residue left after coal is burned to generate electricity. It can contain toxic heavy metals, including mercury, cadmium and arsenic, which can threaten groundwater, soil and rivers.The coal-ash ponds are close to the Ohio River, a drinking-water source for millions of people in the Greater Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky regions. The waste-storage site is also near Clermont County's public drinking-water wells.A separate part of the dispute, involving allegations that CLP failed to disclose information about the handling and movement of coal ash, is yet to go before another jury. Clermont County has also filed a separate lawsuit seeking to force companies linked to the site to clean up the waste.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Fresh US-Israel attack on Iran under consideration as tensions escalate - Report
articles.summary: The United States and Israel are considering launching a fresh military assault on Iran in the coming weeks, CBS News reported on Friday, citing sources
articles.body: The United States and Israel are considering launching a fresh military assault on Iran in the coming weeks, CBS News reported on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. Israel is concerned that Tehran is rapidly rebuilding its ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and moving military and nuclear infrastructure underground.Israel is prepared for another round of fighting and has strengthened its defences against a possible Iranian first strike, the sources told CBS News. However, it remains unclear whether US president Donald Trump is willing to authorise another military operation or what form it could take.Israeli prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration would prefer a joint operation with Washington, but the political costs of renewed fighting could complicate the decision for both leaders. The war was a key factor in the Republicans' defeat in the recent US midterm elections and remains unpopular among American voters.The US has already deployed substantial military assets in the region, including tens of thousands of personnel, two aircraft carriers and their accompanying strike groups. CBS News reported that a new offensive could be launched within two to four days if Trump gave the order.Diplomatic deadlock, rising military tensionsMonths of indirect negotiations between Washington and Tehran have failed to produce a ceasefire agreement that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has refused to discuss its nuclear programme unless the US lifts its naval blockade and accepts a set of other conditions.Trump has repeatedly said Tehran wants a deal but has offered mixed signals about the possibility of renewed military action. In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, he said he wanted an agreement that would last, while warning that he would "finish it off" soon, one way or another.However, speaking to Israel's Channel 12 on Thursday, Trump said he was "not rushing into any decision" and suggested the stalemate could continue into 2027.The possibility of a fresh assault has gained attention following a meeting between US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper and senior Israeli security officials at Israel's defence ministry on Wednesday. The Israeli military described it as a "joint, comprehensive situational assessment".Israel's military chief Eyal Zamir and Mossad director Roman Gofman were among those who met Cooper. Gofman had also travelled to Washington the previous week and met US officials, including CIA director John Ratcliffe, according to people familiar with the matter cited by CBS News.The presence of the Mossad chief at the meeting was unusual and fuelled speculation that Iran was a central topic of discussion.Netanyahu faces political uncertaintyAny decision to resume a major military campaign would come at a politically sensitive time for Netanyahu. His political rivals have been tasked with forming a government following Israel's national election last month, potentially leaving him in office for only a few more weeks.Netanyahu has argued that Israel needs a unity government to confront its security threats, with Iran remaining central to his concerns. However, some of his political opponents suspect he may be using the prospect of renewed conflict to avoid losing power, CBS News reported.Trump had endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the Israeli election and has indicated that he would prefer to work with the Israeli leader in any new operation against Iran.Meanwhile, Trump has raised the possibility that Iran could be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, but has provided no evidence for the allegation. "They're looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," he told a Fox News reporter in China.Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei rejected the allegation on Thursday, comparing it to US claims before the 2003 invasion of Iraq that Saddam Hussein's government was developing weapons of mass destruction. In a post on X, Baqaei described the latest allegations as following a "fraudulent script".Iran has consistently denied seeking to build nuclear weapons. However, after Trump withdrew the US from the 2015 nuclear agreement during his first term, Tehran expanded its uranium enrichment programme beyond levels required for civilian nuclear energy.International monitors believe Iran still has a stockpile of about 900 pounds of uranium enriched to 60% purity, potentially buried beneath the remains of heavily damaged nuclear facilities, according to CBS News.The speculation over a wider military operation comes amid renewed exchanges between Iran and the US. American forces struck Iran's strategic Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. US officials described the strike as an act of self-defence after Iranian attacks targeted American assets in Bahrain, which the US military said were intercepted.Iran also launched strikes against Kuwait this week, though officials said they caused no damage.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Don't reduce it to bilateral': Pakistan minister in Delhi for SCO ducks question on terror
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Pakistan minister Musadik Masood Malik, who is in New Delhi for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan minister Musadik Masood Malik, who is in New Delhi for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, on Friday sidestepped questions on Islamabad's harbouring of terrorists and failure to act against terror networks. He, however, acknowledged that India has suffered terror attacks.Malik, who is leading Pakistan's delegation at the three-day forum, sought to steer questions on cross-border terrorism towards broader regional security concerns, arguing that the SCO platform should not be reduced to bilateral disputes, news agency ANI reported.The minister also called for an evidence-based mechanism to address terrorism, insisting that both sides should present evidence and that discussions should focus on regional challenges rather than accusations.He acknowledged that India, like Pakistan, had suffered terror attacks, but avoided directly addressing questions on terrorist networks operating from Pakistani soil. Malik instead stressed dialogue, mutual understanding and regional cooperation, saying the SCO framework could help address wider security challenges across the neighbourhood."I am here at a multilateral forum. I wish for the discussions at this forum to proceed in a proper and orderly manner. The issues we face are not limited solely to those between our two nations; they have become far broader and more extensive. As you have seen, challenges have emerged in our neighbourhood—in Iran, in Central Asia, and in Afghanistan. I do not wish to reduce such a significant, wide-ranging dialogue to a purely bilateral context," Malik said.When pressed further on cross-border terrorism at a gala dinner following the forum, the Pakistani minister again avoided a direct response, emphasising the need for countries to understand each other's perspectives and engage in constructive dialogue."However, when the time comes to address the issue of terrorism, you are well aware that thousands of our people have been martyred and we must ensure transparency. Both sides must bring forward evidence. Our objective is to establish a transparent mechanism—a proposal we have put forward on several occasions. Such a mechanism would help restore trust and could lead to viable solutions. Often, the necessary evidence is never presented," Malik claimed.Malik also sought to project Pakistan as a constructive regional player, saying Islamabad was committed to participating in efforts aimed at restoring peace and addressing instability.The first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum is being hosted in New Delhi as part of efforts to promote cultural exchange, mutual understanding and people-to-people ties among countries in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.The three-day forum brings together representatives from SCO member countries for discussions on civilisational links, cultural cooperation and regional engagement. Malik's visit marks the first visit by a Pakistani minister to India in three years.Pakistan's delegation is participating in thematic discussions at the forum, which seeks to strengthen cultural and civilisational engagement among SCO countries amid regional geopolitical tensions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Britain's 'mistake of the century'? 10 years after Brexit, UK moves closer to EU, but rejoining won't be easy
articles.summary: Ten years after voting to leave the European Union, Britain appears to be having second thoughts about one of the most consequential decisions in its
articles.body: Ten years after voting to leave the European Union, Britain appears to be having second thoughts about one of the most consequential decisions in its modern history.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has openly questioned the benefits of Brexit, saying Britain has lost more than it gained from the split, while his government moves to rebuild economic ties with Brussels through a series of new agreements.The shift became evident at the UK-EU summit in Brussels on Thursday, where both sides agreed on a fresh set of measures aimed at repairing economic ties strained by Brexit.The agreements cover food and agricultural trade, youth mobility and cooperation on carbon emissions, marking a significant step towards closer relations without Britain formally rejoining the bloc.Under the new arrangements, Britain and the EU will ease checks and paperwork on food products, allow up to 100,000 young people from each side to live, work or study across the Channel for up to three years, and link their carbon emissions trading systems.According to the joint UK-EU statement, the agreements are aimed at reducing barriers to trade, creating opportunities for young people and strengthening cooperation on climate policy.The food and agricultural deal is expected to make trade easier by reducing sanitary and phytosanitary checks, while linking carbon markets could help businesses avoid additional costs associated with carbon border measures.However, the agreements do not signal a reversal of Brexit. Britain will remain outside the EU's single market and customs union, even as both sides seek to restore some of the economic benefits of closer integration.Why is Britain reconsidering Brexit?The renewed push for closer ties comes amid growing criticism of the economic consequences of Britain's departure from the EU.Brexit supporters had promised greater economic freedom, control over immigration and the ability to strike independent trade deals.However, the departure also introduced new barriers to trade with the UK's largest nearby market, increased costs for businesses and restricted the movement of workers between Britain and European countries.According to CNN, economists estimate that Brexit has left Britain's economy between 4 and 8 per cent smaller than it would have been had the country remained in the European Union.Burnham has been particularly vocal in his criticism of the decision. Speaking ahead of the Brussels summit, he compared Brexit to The Emperor's New Clothes, arguing that its promised benefits had failed to materialise.He said Brexit had contributed to Britain's economic difficulties, weakened Europe's position and benefited Russia by deepening divisions among European countries.The economic cost of Brexit has become a major part of the debate. According to CNN, estimates suggest that Britain's economy has lost between 2 per cent and 8 per cent in potential output because of its departure from the EU. The country has also faced additional trade paperwork, higher costs for exporters and restrictions on access to European labour markets.Burnham has argued that the existing arrangement, often described as a 'hard Brexit', is not good enough for Britain. He has also indicated that the latest agreements could contribute up to 0.5 per cent to the country's GDP, while reducing bureaucratic hurdles for businesses.Is Britain preparing to rejoin the European Union?Despite reopening the debate over Brexit, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has stopped short of committing Britain to rejoining the European Union.Following the November 20 summit in Brussels, Burnham said Britain needed to consider what its long-term relationship with the bloc should look like and indicated that he would explore future options with European leaders. However, he has maintained that the latest agreements represent the limit of what his government can achieve during the current parliamentary term.Experts believe that moving towards full membership would be considerably more complicated than restoring trade and diplomatic ties.Anand Menon, professor at King's College London and director of the think tank UK in a Changing Europe, told CNN that Burnham's rhetoric had become more ambitious, but his actual policy approach had not changed significantly from that of his predecessor."The more people talk about rejoining, the more obviously complicated an undertaking it becomes," Menon said, adding that further progress would require Britain to reconsider its existing red lines on European integration.There are also indications that Brussels would not oppose Britain's eventual return, although negotiations could prove difficult.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said she would like to see Britain back in the bloc but warned that Brexit had left considerable mistrust within the European Union."There are still certain traumas in the European Union regarding the UK's departure from the bloc. Therefore, negotiations will not be that easy," she said, according to EU observer.European Council President Antonio Costa also said after the summit that the EU would respect whatever decision Britain takes about its long-term relationship with the bloc.Domestically, Burnham faces opposition from Brexit supporters, including Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who has accused him of having no mandate to move Britain closer to the EU.Public opinion, meanwhile, appears more favourable towards rejoining than it was in 2016, although polling cited by CNN suggests voters remain concerned about the financial contributions, the possibility of adopting the euro and the complexities of another membership application.For now, Britain is seeking closer economic and political cooperation rather than preparing a formal membership bid. Whether that changes will depend on the next general election, public support and the terms Brussels is willing to offer.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 10-year-old in US shoots teen neighbour dead as mothers fight over loud music; watch
articles.summary: A shocking video showing a 10-year-old boy allegedly shooting his teenage neighbour dead during a fight between their mothers over loud music at a
articles.body: A shocking video showing a 10-year-old boy allegedly shooting his teenage neighbour dead during a fight between their mothers over loud music at a Halloween celebration in Albuquerque, New Mexico, has surfaced online.The newly released home security footage, made public by police, shows the boy returning to the scene with a handgun and firing at the teenager while the two women are fighting outside their homes. The incident took place on October 31, but the footage has now emerged on social media after being released by police.The victim was identified as Keinerlein Plaza Rangel, a teenager who had gone to the home of 40-year-old Elaina Gomez-Villeda following a dispute over loud music, the New York Post reported.The video obtained by KOB4 shows Gomez-Villeda, dressed in a Day of the Dead costume with white face paint and flowers in her hair, arguing with her neighbours. The confrontation soon turns physical, with the women punching each other and pulling one another's hair.Gomez-Villeda's son briefly joins the fight, striking one of the neighbours before returning inside the house. He then comes back holding a handgun with both hands and points it at Rangel.The footage shows the boy apparently attempting to fire the weapon, but no shot is discharged initially. After handling the gun for a few seconds, he raises it again and fires. Rangel is struck by a bullet and collapses.The video shows Gomez-Villeda telling her son to get the gun before the shooting. She has been charged with an open count of murder, child abuse and contributing to the delinquency of a minor.Prosecutors are seeking to keep her in custody pending trial, arguing that her actions showed “an extreme disregard for the lives and safety of others”.The boy has not been charged because of his age. Police are working with the district attorney's office and state authorities to determine whether any charges can be brought against him, the NY Post reported.Albuquerque Police Department spokesperson Gilbert Gallegos said investigators were still trying to establish the circumstances surrounding the shooting. “We have no idea what his intent was, what he was doing with the gun, how he got it,” Gallegos said.“They're going to have to figure out what charges, if any, are applicable and what to do with the 10-year-old,” he added.Police said officers responded to reports of a shooting around 4 pm near Tennessee and Copper NE in Albuquerque. articles.title: A woman agreed to buy Harry Kane's former rented London mansion for £16.9 million but failed twice to complete the payment; seller then resold the property for £10.15 million, and court ordered her to pay further damages
articles.summary: A £16.9 million deal to purchase a North London mansion previously rented by footballer Harry Kane collapsed after the prospective buyer failed to
articles.body: A £16.9 million deal to purchase a North London mansion previously rented by footballer Harry Kane collapsed after the prospective buyer failed to complete the transaction twice. The property was eventually sold for approximately £10.15 million, leaving its owner facing a substantial financial shortfall. The dispute between the seller, Regal BA Limited, and buyer Jun Zhang reached the High Court, where the judge examined the failed sale, the property's eventual resale and the evidence used to assess its market value.Why did the £16.9 million Harry Kane mansion sale collapseJun Zhang agreed to buy the North London property from Regal BA Limited for £16.9 million, according to a case summary by the Expert Witness Institute. However, the agreement failed because Zhang did not uphold the deal.The purchase failed, and another attempt to complete the transaction also failed. Regal BA Limited was unable to proceed with the agreed sale at the original price and had to look for another buyer.The dispute was subsequently litigated in Regal BA Limited v Jun Zhang [2026] EWHC 1446 (Ch). The problem was the financial impact of the failed deal, specifically the gap between the price set in the original contract and what was ultimately obtained when the property was sold to a different buyer. The mansion had previously been rented by England football captain Harry Kane. Its association with the footballer added a recognisable name to the property dispute.What happened during the 2 failed completion attemptsThe court judgment provides a detailed account of how the agreement unfolded. Regal had agreed to sell the 7 bedroom property called High Trees to Zhang on 23 March 2022. The contract valued the house at £16.85 million, with £50,000 extra for its contents.On the same day, Zhang signed a tenancy agreement and moved into the property with her partner, Stuart Onslow, and their two children. It then changed the original completion date to 27 September 2023 with a deposit of £1.685 million which would be lost if the purchase did not go ahead.But Zhang failed to close the transaction by the extended deadline. On 19 December 2023 Regal ended the agreement and kept the deposit.On the same day, the two sides entered into another agreement, but keeping the overall purchase price at £16.9 million. This time the deposit was increased to £2,527,500 and completion was set for 22 April 2024.The second attempt also failed. Zhang did not complete the purchase by the agreed date, and Regal served a formal notice giving her another 10 working days to fulfil the contract. That additional period expired on 8 May 2024 without completion. The second agreement was subsequently terminated, and Regal retained the new deposit as well.How did Regal attempt to sell the mansion againAfter the second failed transaction, Regal had to find another purchaser for High Trees. The company began marketing the property through specialist estate agents, including Sotheby's International Realty and DDRE Global, with an asking price of £16.5 million.The marketing campaign involved outreach to potential buyers in the UK and internationally. The court judgment said this had resulted in some 10 to 12 viewings of the property but the agents had struggled to get an offer anywhere near the asking price.The market was also difficult for expensive London homes at the time. Feedback from potential buyers highlighted concerns about the property's privacy, its position near the road and the absence of certain features, including a lift and a larger garden.One prospective buyer indicated that the property would be attractive at around £9 million to £10 million. Other interested parties decided against purchasing for reasons related to the house's layout and location.Regal eventually agreed to sell the mansion to 16 Bishop Limited for £10,157,168.94. The transaction was completed on 12 September 2024, several months after Zhang's second failure to complete.Zhang challenged the resale priceZhang accepted that Regal was entitled to compensation for the failed purchase but disputed the amount being claimed. Her argument was that the company had sold the mansion for considerably less than its actual market value.As reported by the Expert Witness Institute, Zhang's property valuation expert estimated that High Trees was worth £14.75 million in September 2024. This was substantially higher than the £10.15 million resale price.Her legal team also questioned whether Regal had marketed the property for long enough to secure a better offer. They argued that the company had already been in discussions with the eventual buyer while the property was being advertised elsewhere.Another point raised during the proceedings concerned a separate proposed £3 million loan involving companies connected to the eventual purchaser. Zhang argued that the arrangement could have influenced Regal's decision to accept a lower price.However, Regal maintained that the sale was conducted properly and that the resale figure reflected the offers available in a challenging market.How did the High Court assess the evidenceJudge Hacon examined the marketing efforts, the competing property valuations and the circumstances surrounding the eventual sale. He concluded that Regal had given the mansion an appropriate period of exposure through two successive specialist estate agencies. The property had been marketed for a combined period of around 7 to 8 months.The judge also noted that the top end of the London property market was struggling in 2024. His feeling was that in delaying he was more likely to get a lower offer than a higher one.The court was not persuaded that Regal had deliberately sold the mansion below its available market value. It found that the property had been sold competently, through an open-market process and at arm's length.What compensation did the court award RegalIn its ruling, the High Court accepted Regal's main claim for the difference between the £16.9 million contract price and the £10.1 million resale price. However, the amount was subject to deductions.The judge deducted the £2,527,500 deposit retained after the second failed completion. He also reduced the claim by £1 million because the original deal stated that Regal should have paid that amount toward Zhang’s Stamp Duty Land Tax if she had bought the property on time. After these deductions the main damages were approximately £3.22 million.The court also took into account other financial losses, such as interest paid on Regal’s outstanding loan from Deutsche Bank from May through September 2024. Judge Hacon allowed interest calculated on the reduced loan balance, taking into account that the company should have used both forfeited deposits to reduce its borrowing.Regal was also awarded £13,092.10 in professional fees connected with the resale, along with interest at 4% on the sums allowed by the court.You use AI every day. articles.title: ICE spent $13 million a month for empty beds, government watchdog reports
articles.summary: ICE spent an estimated $13 million a month for empty beds at five recently acquired detention centers and overpaid by more than 50% for nine megawarehouses — most of which the immigration enforcement agency is now trying to offload, according to a new report from the government’s watchdog.
articles.body: ICE spent an estimated $13 million a month for empty beds at five recently acquired detention centers and overpaid by more than 50% for nine megawarehouses — most of which the immigration enforcement agency is now trying to offload, according to a new report from the government’s watchdog. In total, ICE spent more than $1 billion in taxpayer money on the warehouses. According to the report, ICE paid more than triple the assessed value for three of the warehouses. In Michigan, ICE bought a warehouse for more than $34 million, which the Government Accountability Office calculated was nearly five times the assessed value. ICE did not respond to NBC News’ request for comment. The immigration agency responded to the GAO within the report and agreed with the report’s recommendations that it should keep its spending plans updated and evaluate the full cost of a detention facility’s cost before purchase. In its letter to the watchdog, DHS wrote that the agency “remains committed to ICE strengthening the necessary processes, policies, procedures, and safeguards to ensure the continual oversight and management of ICE’s financial resources as it carries out its mission.” Roughly a year ago, ICE began exploring a plan to buy massive empty warehouses to house up to 8,000 immigrant detainees each, but the plan quickly ran into roadblocks when local leaders, immigrant advocates and some GOP members of Congress expressed sharp opposition. Plans for one ICE warehouse in the Atlanta suburb of Social Circle, Georgia, sparked a lawsuit in which town officials said the new facility would exceed the capacity of the town’s sewage system and result in “dry taps and raw human waste spills.” Contractors from private prison companies also expressed concern about housing more than 1,500 detainees in one location. After then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s departure from the agency in late March, the agency paused the warehouse plan. Now at least seven warehouses are for sale, according to the report. The authors of the GAO report wrote that the warehouse initiative was an example of a “major investment that was implemented rapidly and will likely result in significant waste.” ICE has roughly doubled the number of detention facilities it manages but is facing a shortfall in staff who oversee and manage those facilities. Fifty-five out of 87 positions are currently vacant, according to the report. On average, ICE paid for more than 9,000 empty beds per day across facilities with guaranteed-payment agreements, the report found. ICE began purchasing new detention capacity after the July 2025 passage of President Donald Trump’s “big beautiful bill,” which gave the agency $45 billion through 2029. ICE also faced scrutiny for paying $495 million for a former prison in western Minnesota, a year after its owner offered to sell the same facility to the state for $75 million, according to documents obtained by KARE 11. Democrats on the House Homeland Security Committee sent a letter to DHS on Friday asking for documents related to that sale.
