articles.title: A North Carolina couple noticed their new home's kitchen floor dipping within weeks of moving in in 2016, then sued the builder years later; an appeals court has rejected their defective-construction claims
articles.summary: A North Carolina couple noticed that their new home's kitchen floor had a major dip within weeks of moving in in 2016.
articles.body: A North Carolina couple noticed that their new home's kitchen floor had a major dip within weeks of moving in in 2016. They contacted the builder, and a representative came to the house to stabilise the affected area. But years later, after consulting a contractor, they became concerned that the house had been built on an improperly sloped foundation.The couple eventually sued the builder in January 2025, seeking damages over alleged construction defects. However, the North Carolina Court of Appeals has rejected their claims, ruling that they waited too long to take legal action and did not provide enough evidence to support some of their other allegations, according to Law Justia.In its November 18, 2026, judgment in Holton v. Value Build Homes, the court upheld an earlier decision granting summary judgment to the builders. The case was brought by Nate Holton and Christine Holton against Value Build Homes and related companies.Floor problem appeared shortly after moving inAccording to the court's judgment, the couple signed a contract with Value Build Homes on November 15, 2015, for the construction of a house in Moore County, North Carolina. The home received its certificate of occupancy on May 17, 2016, allowing the couple to move in.Within 30 to 60 days, they noticed what the court described as a “substantial dip in the kitchen floor”. They contacted the builders, and a representative visited the property and stabilised the affected area.The couple also signed an application for a builder's limited warranty with Professional Warranty Service Corporation on October 14, 2016. The warranty provided different levels of coverage for 10 years from May 17, 2016, and required disputes to be settled through binding arbitration.The issue came up again in October 2023, when the couple consulted a crawlspace contractor. They became concerned that the house had been built on an improperly sloped foundation.On November 8, 2023, Nate Holton contacted the builders and said, “The house was never level since day 1.” The builders investigated the complaint in 2024, excavating near the foundation and taking measurements. The couple filed their lawsuit on January 17, 2025. They accused the companies of breach of contract, breach of express and implied warranties, defective construction, negligence and unfair and deceptive trade practices.Why the court rejected the claimsThe couple argued that the six-year legal deadline should be counted from 2023, when they became concerned about the foundation, rather than from 2016, when the house was completed. But the appeals court disagreed. It said the home was substantially complete no later than May 17, 2016, the date its certificate of occupancy was issued. North Carolina law generally does not allow claims over defective construction to be filed more than six years after substantial completion or the relevant last act or omission by the defendant.The court also rejected the argument that the builders' later involvement extended this period. It found that the couple had not provided evidence that the builders carried out repairs after 2016 under the original construction contract. Their work in 2024 involved investigating the complaint and taking measurements, not repairing the house.The couple also relied on the 10-year structural warranty. However, the judges said they had not identified a specific warranty provision that the builders had breached or shown evidence of a particular obligation imposed on them. The warranty was administered through Professional Warranty Service Corporation, against which the couple had voluntarily dismissed their claims with prejudice in April 2026.The court therefore concluded that the construction-related claims were filed outside the six-year period. It also considered the separate time limits for filing lawsuits. Contract and negligence claims had a three-year limitation period, while the unfair and deceptive trade practices claim had a four-year period.The judges said the couple knew about the floor problem in 2016 because they had noticed the dip and contacted the builders. They did not need to know the exact cause or full extent of the defect for the legal time limit to begin. The couple waited more than eight years after discovering the problem to file their lawsuit.Court also rejects negligence and deception claimsThe couple's negligence claim argued that the builders had failed to construct the home properly and sought compensation for the loss in the property's value and the cost of repairs. The court rejected this claim under North Carolina's economic loss rule. It said the couple had not identified a duty owed by the builders that was separate from their contractual obligations. Since the damages involved financial losses arising from the alleged failure to meet the construction contract, they could not be recovered through a negligence claim.The couple also accused the builders of concealing the defect and making inaccurate statements about the foundation. The court said that even if these allegations were true, they had not shown a separate financial loss caused by the alleged deception. The damages they sought were the same as those claimed for the construction problems.The ruling does not establish that the house had no construction defects. It means the couple's claims could not proceed because of the legal time limits and the lack of evidence needed to support their remaining allegations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Poppy Jay: An exhausting two days in the shoes of a British tradwife
articles.summary: Writer and broadcaster Poppy Jay tries living as a British tradwife for a documentary, and speaks to BBC News.
articles.body:
Dressed in an unfamiliar long skirt, Poppy Jay is standing in a chicken coop faced with an angry cockerel as she checks for eggs.

As a director and writer, Jay is normally behind the camera, but today she's in front of it, trying out life as a tradwife.

The Tradwife - short for traditional wife - movement sees women embracing traditional gender roles in the home, such as cooking, cleaning and child rearing, while submitting to their bread-winning husbands.

While tradwives say they are bringing back old-fashioned family values, the movement has faced controversy. Its critics say tradwives fuel inequality and diminish women's empowerment by reinforcing archetypal gender roles.

For three days, Evangelical Christians Molly and Aaron Edwards welcomed Jay, a proud feminist, into their Yorkshire home to show her their lifestyle for the BBC One documentary Young, British and Tradwife .

On two of the days, the couple - who have seven children - allowed Jay to take on the homely duties that are usually Molly's responsibility, so Jay could try out the tradwife life.

"I was exhausted," Jay exclaimed when she spoke to BBC News.

During her stay, she helped Molly cook, home school the children, tend to the garden and brave the chicken coop.

She was given a book called The Gift of Womanhood to study the night before and asked to wear a dress.

"What struck me was how hard Molly works - like any mum of seven," Jay said. "She is a devoted mother, she cooks and cleans, she's doing endless loads of washing. She's barely got a moment to herself and I felt like I was getting in the way."

The tradwife phenomenon has been popularised on social media which has been a major driving force in its expansion.

Some US creators have millions of followers - Hannah Neeleman, widely seen as one of the world's leading tradwife influencers, has 10.3 million users following her Instagram account, Ballerina Farm.

However, another popular American influencer, Nara Smith, has rejected the label. Smith married young, has four children and her content centres on cooking food (or even making toothpaste) from scratch, but insists she's no tradwife.

"They kind of used me as the poster child of the tradwife movement, which was very bizarre to me," Smith said on the Call Her Daddy podcast. "Sure, do I love cooking... but that's a passion of mine, it's a hobby - it's not something that I need to be doing."

The tradwife trend has also made its way into popular culture, with author Caro Claire Burke's satirical novel Yesteryear selling more than 1.4 million copies and Hollywood actress Anne Hathaway has signed up to produce and star in a film adaptation.

Much of the tradwife lifestyle is played out on social media with glossy images of baking and planting vegetables, but Molly Edwards has been a tradwife for more than 15 years, long before TikToks existed.

She sees the role as more than "just floating around in a dress, baking sourdough".

"It's very connected to our faith," she explains in the documentary, "and what we believe God has designed women to do and to be in their homes, just under the guidance and leadership of our husbands."

Jay tells BBC News she saw how much work Molly did which had "parallels" with her upbringing in a conservative Muslim family, which included her entering an arranged marriage when she was 19. She and her husband divorced about five years later.

"I've helped raise my siblings, I know my way around a kitchen, I can cook, I tutored my siblings," Jay said. "Other than the chicken coop, it's not unfamiliar territory. But I think doing it for two days - I know this sounds ridiculous... it's just the relentless pace of her life."

While Molly manages the house, her husband Aaron is a full-time theologian who shares his views on religion and anti-feminism on social media.

When speaking to Jay, Aaron explained the reason the household work was down to his wife: "Molly's obviously omni-competent and brilliant but submission is still really hard," he says, "and when I say something that Molly disagrees with, that's when the submission really matters."

"It happens at least once a month where something will happen where Molly will have a certain idea… it might be something trivial like how we should organise the day and I might have a bigger vision where I go, 'No, that's been overridded.'"

Jay admits that during her interviews with Aaron, there was some "sparring", with the pair often not seeing eye-to-eye.

"He doesn't like feminism," Jay said, "he thinks feminism's ruined society."

"He definitely romanticises a bygone era, which I think [means] you're going down a dangerous path. [He had] the idea that women were better off in the Victorian times - according to who? What evidence do you have of that?"

While Molly says her social media does not make money, some tradwives do look to turn a profit through their posts.

West Sussex couple Megan and Joseph Landreth-Smith have three children and have an Instagram account with nearly 6,000 followers.

Megan often gets brand deals to share products on her Instagram, which she says helps with some extra income and "feels like a really natural fit" around what they are doing already - producing content while being with their children.

Just like many influencers, trolls can be a problem, but they also help to bring in some money.

With her husband Zion, Yorkshire-based life coach Laura Zachary promotes a course called the Academy of Biblical Wifery, based on their born-again Christian beliefs, to more than 32,000 Instagram followers.

"The more disagreement on a comments section, the more people that come to it and the more you get paid".

In a busy and complicated world, Jay said she appreciates why some women see the attraction in living in what seems to be a more simple way as a tradwife.

But after a few days of experiencing a tradwife's role, she was exhausted and frustrated, saying the belief that men were in charge of everything was "where I draw the line".

"I came away having a lot of respect for [Molly] and to a degree understanding the appeal," Jay said, "but I think for me the submission was the hardest part to grapple with and seeing submission in real life play out in front of me - that was an interesting experience."

The "appeal" which Jay identifies goes much broader - a report published by King's College London found 79% of women surveyed were drawn to the relaxed, calm lifestyle it portrays.

But its co-author, Prof Heejung Chung, who specialises in researching the tradwife phenomenon, said that it can be the tip of a political change.

The content might begin with "nice dresses", said Chung, but can "draw them towards more extremist, far-right, or nationalist ideologies, which ultimately seek to curtail women's autonomy and reinforce patriarchal authority".

However, her report concludes most young women and men surveyed showed "largely progressive views on gender roles".

For those who liked the content, it was down to its "lifestyle imagery", rather than "the traditional gender division of labour or power".

But this does not mean the tradwife movement poses no risk to gender equality, the report says, and its "growing popularity... should not be dismissed or trivialised".

articles.title: South Africa's local elections: ANC fights to keep control of cities after election setback
articles.summary: The ANC appears reluctant to replicate its national power-sharing deal with the pro-business DA at the local level.
articles.body:
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.

The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.

Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.

While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.

Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.

It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.

The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.

It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.

The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.

Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?

The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.

The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).

Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.

Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.

The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.

Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.

In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.

The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.

ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.

Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?

It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.

While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.

A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.

While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.

Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".

Would coalition governments improve services?

The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.

While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.

But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.

Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.

As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.

This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.

"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.

Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

articles.title: 'Enough': Protesters decry antisemitism after Hunter College student event including Jewish group is canceled
articles.summary: Pro-Israel rally organizers at Hunter College say the cancelled Cultural Arts Night shows antisemitism at CUNY, as counter protesters chant nearby.
articles.body: A crowd gathered Thursday outside Hunter College to protest after the school's student government seemingly canceled an event due to the participation of a Jewish organization. On one side of the street, pro-Israel protesters chanted "enough is enough" and waved American and Israeli flags as speakers addressed the crowd. Across the street, a group of counter-protesters gathered waving Palestinian flags while yelling chants of their own. Passersby also shouted, some in support and others yelling "Free Palestine" and "F--- Israel." JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS Organizers behind the Stand with Jewish Students at Hunter rally included the Israeli American Council (IAC), Students Supporting Israel (SSI) and #EndJewHatred. On flyers advertising the rally, they criticized the college's administration for not doing enough in response to what they saw as an act of antisemitism. "We're saying enough to the marginalization of the Jewish community. We're saying enough is enough to discrimination against Jewish students. And we're saying enough is enough to this obsessive hatred of all of the symbols of Jewish life, whether it's Hillel on campus or the State of Israel," IAC CEO Elan Carr told Fox News Digital, referring to a chapter of the Jewish student group. Michelle Ahdoot, director of programming and strategy at #EndJewHatred, told Fox News Digital the cancellation of the event demonstrated a problem that went beyond Hunter College. "When a multicultural event is canceled simply because Jewish students are included, we have a serious problem that goes far beyond one event at Hunter College," Ahdoot said. "The very purpose of multiculturalism is to celebrate diversity and inclusion, not to allow certain groups to decide who is welcome and who is not. "Any student organization has the right to choose not to participate," he continued. "But when an elected student government responds by canceling the entire event rather than standing up for the inclusion of Jewish students, it sends a dangerous message that Jewish participation is somehow unacceptable." The Cultural Arts Night was scheduled to take place Nov. 16 but was canceled just days before. Hunter College Undergraduate Student Government (USG) flyers promoting the event showed that clubs involved included Students for Justice in Palestine, the Peruvian Student Association, Hunter Chinese Student & Scholar Association, the Taiwanese Student Association and Hunter Hillel, according to screenshots posted online. Hillel International is a Jewish organization that can be found on college campuses across the globe. It describes itself as "a space for all kinds of Jewish students — a place where they feel welcomed and included." While its vision includes helping students make "an enduring commitment to Jewish life, learning and Israel," it is focused on Jewish life and culture, hosting holidays and holding events. FIRE ALARM DISRUPTS NORTHWESTERN 'OCTOBER 7' PLAY BASED ON MASSACRE SURVIVOR TESTIMONY Rita Levine Rabin Hillel at Hunter College said in a statement on Instagram it was "looking forward" to the event and that it "had no role in the decision to cancel." "Antisemitism has no place at Hunter College. Jewish students should never be singled out, scapegoated, or made to feel unwelcome because of who they are and the anti-Semitic response online to the cancellation notice has been egregious and inappropriate," the statement read. Ilya Bratman, who serves as executive director at Hillel at Baruch College in New York City, said the cancellation of Cultural Arts Night was a clear case of antisemitism and a sign that things could escalate. "This is so obvious, and antisemitism has nothing to do with Israel. And that's what the main thing you have to say very loudly. This is about Jew hatred and exclusion," Bratman told Fox News Digital. "It's the first step in the process, which begins with physical exclusion of Jewish students from campuses. "And that is what happened in the 1930s. We know this. This is a slower process here in American campuses, and I believe this is going to keep going if we don't step up in a very serious way to stop it." Hunter College USG announced the cancellation on Nov. 14 in a statement from Hunter College USG President Sumaiya Ahmed and Vice President Ahmad Waraich. The two student leaders claimed that "lapses in communication kept the details of this event from reaching the people at the top." "We hear what the student body has said, and we have made the decision to cancel the event as it doesn’t align with our values or the values of the students we represent as the Hunter Community. We apologize to the clubs and students who were affected by this instance," a statement posted on Instagram read. After the announcement, speculation about the reason for the event's cancellation grew, with some pointing to pressure from anti-Israel activists who objected to Hillel's involvement. While this was not directly addressed, Hunter USG appeared to deny it in a subsequent statement in which it said that the event was canceled over "safety concerns." BIPARTISAN DUO LAUNCHES CONGRESSIONAL CAUCUS TO CONFRONT ANTISEMITISM AT COLLEGES Hunter College is a public institution in the City University of New York (CUNY) system, making allegations of discrimination particularly serious since public schools are legally barred from discriminating based on religion or national origin. Hunter College told Fox News Digital it was "deeply troubled by reports that some student groups pulled from the event because of Hillel’s participation" and said it was investigating the issue. "There is no place for discrimination and harassment in our college community. We have policies in place to safeguard that principle and will not hesitate to enforce them," the college said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. Michal Mari, who is president of SSI at Hunter College, told Fox News Digital during the rally that the environment at the school has been "tough" for Jewish students. She said Jewish students had seen calls for violence against their community, including statements calling to "bring the war home" and "globalize the intifada." Mari believes the cancellation came after clubs dropped out of the event due to Hillel's participation, which she said was "blatant discrimination against Jewish students on campus." "I've had professors turn their backs to me while I was speaking to them because they found out that I was wearing a Star of David or that I've been to Israel," Mari told Fox News Digital. "So, it's certainly not the most divided, but it's a place where there's work to be done." Mari addressed the crowd at Thursday night's rally along with a number of other pro-Israel and Jewish speakers, including Shai Davidai, Ari Ackerman, Shabbos Kestenbaum and Rami Matan Even-Esh (also known as Kosha Dillz), among others, including Hunter College students. Jayne Zirkle, who serves as director of communications for #EndJewHatred, said the organization was "incredibly proud" of the students who chose to speak publicly despite the pressures they face on campus. "Their courage matters, and they deserve to know they are not standing alone," Zirkle said. Davidai, a former Columbia University professor, told Fox News Digital he attended the rally to bring attention to what he saw as the "symptom" of a bigger issue. "The symptom of canceling an event because a Jewish organization is part of it, that is a problem. And, by the way, it's a problem not just for Jews, it's a problem for everyone. Because when you cancel an event, everyone, Jewish or non-Jews, don't get to go to that event," Davidai said. LEO TERRELL TAKES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S ANTISEMITISM FIGHT NATIONWIDE ON 15-CITY TOUR While Davidai focused on the broader cultural fallout on campus, Kestenbaum, a former Harvard Divinity School student who sued Harvard over campus antisemitism, framed the issue around civil rights law and public funding. "You cannot violate civil rights law. Colleges don't get to pick and choose which statute of the Civil Rights Act they want to subscribe to. There is one standard for all universities across the country, and if those universities insist on discriminating against students because of their ethnicity or because of their religious identity, that is illegal," Kestenbaum told Fox News Digital. Kestenbaum is not the only one who has brought up the possible legal issues with canceling the event. New York City Council Member Eric Dinowitz publicly called for a civil rights investigation. "[Hunter College] USG cancels a multicultural arts event because it did not align with its 'values.' It appears to be yet another chapter in the troubling history of antisemitism at CUNY and Hunter," Dinowitz wrote on X. "That's why [CUNY] must immediately launch a Title VI investigation." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Along with calls for institutional and legal accountability, speakers at Thursday night's rally encouraged students at Hunter College not to retreat from campus life and stay silent. "Every student at Hunter or anywhere else, if you speak up, and when you speak up, we've got your back," Davidai said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "We've got your back with numbers. We've got your back with legal support. We got your back on social media. We have got your backs. But it's up to you to speak up, because if you don't speak up then, you know, the word doesn't come out." Mari echoed the message, saying that the Jewish community at Hunter College was ready to rally behind those who choose to speak out. "Courage isn't lack of fear but acting in the face of fear," Mari told Fox News Digital. "You have a community behind you. The Jewish community, especially, is one that is always behind you." articles.title: Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
articles.summary: Copenhagen accuses Moscow of planning assassination with banned local gang; Russia says no evidence for allegation.
articles.body:
Denmark has said it is expelling Russia’s defence attaché after accusing Moscow intelligence of plotting to kill a Ukrainian rapper at a concert near Copenhagen.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attaché from Denmark” within seven days, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference on Friday.

Denmark is also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians, he added.

The expulsion ultimatum comes hours after Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said it suspected Russia of planning the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb with help of a Danish gang.

Danish public broadcaster DR named the rapper as Kyivstoner, who has both Ukrainian and US citizenship.

“A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia,” PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told journalists on Friday.

“The case shows, in our assessment, that the Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out an execution in Denmark,” he said.

According to PET, three people were stopped in a car near the music venue where the rapper was scheduled to perform on September 25. Police found firearms and knives in the vehicle.

Two people were placed under formal investigation on Friday for attempted murder and for helping a foreign intelligence service operate in Denmark. Police and PET suspect Loyal to Familia, a street gang and criminal network banned since 2021, helped plan the attack.

Police and intelligence services made their announcements as two Danish men appeared ⁠in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder, court documents showed.

According to the court documents, the suspects were arrested five minutes before the concert was set to begin and one of them had bought a ticket to the performance. The ‌concert was cancelled.

In response to Friday’s announcement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said, “We are facing a cornered Russia, acting more aggressively and with a greater propensity to take risks.” The strongest response would be to “not waver” and to keep supporting Ukraine, she added.

European Council President Antonio Costa said the alleged assassination attempt was “unacceptable” and “will not go unanswered”. He promised Denmark the European Union’s full backing against what he called Russian hybrid attacks.

Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would give “an appropriate response”, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen called the expulsion “vengeful” and said Denmark had not presented “any evidence of Russia’s involvement in this mysterious crime”.

Copenhagen has accused Moscow of other hybrid attacks, which are acts short of open war, such as sabotage and disruption. In September 2025, drones shut down Copenhagen airport for hours, in what Denmark called a hybrid attack.

PET said in September that Russia was recruiting Danish citizens to help plan sabotage against Danish defence firms with ties to Ukraine.

Russia has denied involvement in such operations.

articles.title: Vote on 'leaving UK' over RAF Barnham migrant housing plans
articles.summary: Barnham is proposing breaking away from the UK in protest of plans to house migrants at RAF Barnham.
articles.body:
Villagers will head to the polls on Saturday to decide whether or not to symbolically leave the UK over plans to house migrants at a former military base.

RAF Barnham, between Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, and Thetford, Norfolk, has been earmarked by the government as a potential base for up to 931 migrants.

The proposals have not gone down well with locals and far-right groups alike, sparking several anti-asylum demonstrations since the summer.

One way or another, residents are now poised to make their voices heard by taking part in a referendum to decide whether to symbolically secede from the country or remain.

Here is everything you need to know about the controversy that has thrust a tiny, otherwise unassuming village into the national spotlight.

The Home Office first floated the idea of using three Ministry of Defence (MoD) sites to house thousands of asylum seekers in June.

Facilities in Bicester in Oxfordshire, Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire, and Barnham in Suffolk were identified to help move people out of hotels.

As of March this year, 20,885 (21%) asylum seekers were living in hotels, while 72,768 (75%) were in other accommodation as they awaited decisions.

The Home Office initially sought to house 1,250 migrants at RAF Barnham, but that number has since been reduced to just shy of 1,000.

According to the government, they would be "single adult males" aged between 18 and 65 years old who could be permitted to leave the site.

If planning permission is granted and the proposals go ahead, "a specialist and experienced provider of security services" would be "permanently on site 24/7".

It is also hoped that there will be enough "essential services" to reduce "the need for asylum seekers to leave the site".

The Home Office, which could use a fast-track planning route to bypass local council permission, is said to have awarded a £3.4m contract for the project to Kier.

The construction giant has been hired to design the camp at the former nuclear weapons store, which has most recently been used for police training.

How do residents feel about the proposals?

The site is located just over a mile away from its namesake village, nearly two miles from Thetford, and close to four miles from Elveden by road.

The plans have been met with strong opposition from local councillors and residents, such as Kim Dines, who has lived in the village for 13 years.

She previously said she had been "lying awake at night" wondering what may result from migrants being housed "so close".

"We're a village of roughly 600 people; we shouldn't be living in fear, we shouldn't be worried about what's going to be on our doorstep [and] who's around us," she said.

Ann Houston said the presence of migrants nearby might alter "the atmosphere in the village".

"Barnham is a place where you can leave your doors open at the moment, and that might change," she said.

Concerns have also been raised about the government's commitment to spend £3.4m on drawing up the scheme before a final decision has been made.

Helen Beck, chairwoman of the Barnham Residents Association, said: "At the moment they don't even know whether it can legally go ahead - hugely disappointing."

John Bauer, chairman of Barnham Parish Council, said leading the campaign against the plans was ruining his retirement .

"I retired at the end of last year with the expectation I would be able to do a lot of the things that I had been looking forward to doing for a while," he said.

"Unfortunately, that hasn't happened. It is demanding and exhausting, and it is not necessarily what I would have chosen to do in [my retirement]."

What would leaving the UK actually mean for Barnham?

In many respects, voting to break away from the UK would very much act as a symbolic gesture and a way for the village to demonstrate its strength of feeling.

That is because there is no legal mechanism allowing the likes of Barnham to declare independence from the UK.

Yes, quite recently, in fact – and for similar reasons.

In September, villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, in Oxfordshire voted to become independent of the UK .

Like in Barnham, it was held in protest against plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.

On that occasion, out of 312 votes cast, 285 people voted to leave, 26 voted no, and one ballot paper was spoiled.

When and where is the referendum taking place and who can vote?

Voting is taking place at Barnham Village Hall from 10:00 GMT to 16:00, before counting gets underway and the result is announced between 17:00 and 18:00.

The council cannot be completely sure how many people will be eligible to vote, due to being unable to use the electoral register, but believes up to 500 could take part.

In the interests of accessibility, some sealed votes will be collected by the council, which has also taken note of those who require help getting to the polling station.

The Home Office said it was "listening carefully to the concerns" of residents and that no decision had yet been taken.

A spokesperson said: "The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

"We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised."

articles.title: Can Africa’s new credit rating agency change how the continent is assessed?
articles.summary: The new African agency aims to bring greater transparency to credit ratings.
articles.body:
Abuja, Nigeria – On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), bringing to fruition an initiative first endorsed by African leaders in 2017.

The agency, based in Port Louis, Mauritius, is designed to provide independent assessments of African governments and corporate borrowers, drawing on local data and expertise to complement ratings issued by international agencies. Its first sovereign ratings are expected by the end of March.

Its interim chief executive, Sifiso Falala, says AfCRA is already in discussions with 15 African governments with research planned in countries that include Mauritius, Kenya, Togo, the Seychelles and Burundi.

The case for AfCRA rests partly on the cost of how African economies are perceived by financial markets. A 2023 study by the United Nations Development Programme estimated that subjectivities in sovereign credit ratings cost African countries $74.5bn through excessive interest payments and foregone lending.

African governments have long argued that international rating methodologies do not adequately account for the continent’s economic structures and circumstances.

The major international agencies – Moody’s, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings – have disputed suggestions that their assessments systematically disadvantage African borrowers. At a Chatham House discussion in June, Moody’s Marie Diron argued that the agency’s analysis of four decades of global sovereign default data showed that African countries with a particular rating had broadly the same probability of default as equally rated borrowers elsewhere.

For example, she said, a sovereign with a B rating had an estimated one-year default probability of about 5 percent regardless of whether it was African or from another region.

That is an important counterargument. AfCRA’s challenge will not simply be to produce different ratings but to demonstrate that its assessments are more comprehensive, transparent and predictive of actual credit risk. Its credibility will ultimately depend on the evidence behind its conclusions, including when those conclusions are unfavourable to African borrowers.

For Falala, the agency’s priority is to ensure that assessments better reflect the economic realities of African countries.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, he said: “A significant number of African countries carry speculative-grade ratings despite having no history of sovereign default.

“This raises legitimate questions about whether prevailing models adequately capture African economic realities. We believe our analytical framework can contribute to a constructive reassessment of these assumptions, encouraging the entire industry to examine whether the indicators used to determine creditworthiness remain relevant, proportionate and sufficiently predictive of actual default risk.”

Falala said the agency was not seeking more favourable ratings for African borrowers but greater accuracy through engagement with established rating agencies.

“Our objective is not to manufacture better ratings for Africa, but to produce more accurate ratings of Africa in collaboration with established rating agencies. Importantly, we believe that a stronger AfCRA will contribute to a stronger credit rating industry overall,” he said.

That distinction will be central to the agency’s credibility. An institution established partly in response to dissatisfaction with existing ratings must demonstrate that its own assessments are independent of political pressure and the interests of the governments and companies it evaluates.

Falala acknowledged the scepticism surrounding the industry, saying AfCRA has an opportunity to rebuild confidence through transparency and analytical independence. He said the agency was not seeking confrontation with established rating providers but saw considerable scope for collaboration and mutual learning.

Beyond sovereign ratings, AfCRA intends to assess companies, municipalities, banks and local-currency debt. This broader coverage could address gaps in information about borrowers that receive limited attention from international agencies while providing domestic investors with additional assessments of credit risk.

The potential benefits extend beyond the ratings themselves. African pension funds, banks and other institutional investors need reliable information to assess domestic borrowers and allocate capital. More comprehensive coverage, supported by stronger local data, could help reduce information gaps and support the development of domestic capital markets.

However, additional ratings will not automatically translate into cheaper borrowing. Their influence will depend on whether investors consider the assessments credible and useful in making investment decisions.

Abdussalam Muazu, an associate chartered economist at the Institute of Chartered Economists of Nigeria, said limited information about African borrowers has contributed to the uncertainty investors factor into lending decisions.

“African governments and companies often pay more to borrow than their ratings suggest, partly because investors know too little about them and price in the uncertainty.

“The big agencies have few analysts on the ground, and much of Africa’s economy runs through informal trade, mobile money and community finance that is hard to measure from outside. An African agency can bring local knowledge into credit ratings and help build the data that is missing today, which gives investors less reason to charge for guesswork,” he told Al Jazeera.

The argument points to a wider problem: The availability and quality of economic data can shape how creditworthiness is assessed. Informal economic activity, for example, is not always adequately captured in conventional indicators, even though it contributes significantly to livelihoods and economic activity across the continent.

Methodology is another part of the debate. Different approaches to assessing sovereign risk can produce different conclusions about the same country’s ability and willingness to meet its financial obligations. AfCRA, therefore, will need to explain clearly how its models account for factors that may be overlooked or insufficiently reflected in existing assessments.

Dayo Obisan, a financial market professional, told Al Jazeera that African countries need rating methodologies that better reflect their economic circumstances and their access to capital.

“The compelling question is how does Africa ensure its peculiarities are factored into the determination of its perception as a sovereign and its access to much-needed capital, which rides on this perception?”

He said an African rating institution could bring greater understanding of these circumstances through its presence across the continent, improved data and methodologies that complement existing approaches.

“The value proposition for the creation of an Africa-focused credit rating agency centres on richer local data, contextual insight, wider coverage and support for domestic markets,” Obisan said.

Independence and credibility under scrutiny

But local knowledge alone will not be enough. AfCRA will also have to demonstrate that its methodology is rigorous, consistent and transparent and its ratings can withstand scrutiny from investors beyond the continent.

Its ownership and financing arrangements will also be important. The agency describes itself as privately owned and self-funded while its planned sovereign assessments will operate on a solicited basis, meaning governments pay for ratings and provide access to officials and financial information.

This is a model also used by established rating agencies, but it makes safeguards against conflicts of interest particularly important. The African Union says governments may not own shares in AfCRA, but the agency will still need to demonstrate that commercial relationships with the borrowers it assesses cannot influence its analytical decisions.

Ultimately, AfCRA’s credibility will not be determined by how many African countries it rates or how far its assessments differ from those of Moody’s, S&P and Fitch.

It will depend on whether investors trust its analyses, whether its methodology withstands scrutiny and, above all, whether it can remain independent when its findings are politically inconvenient.

Its defining test may come when an African government rejects an unfavourable assessment and the agency refuses to change it.

As Falala put it, “What strengthens AfCRA should ultimately strengthen the credibility of the entire credit rating industry. Africa needs more credible assessments, not competing narratives.”

articles.title: Trump calls for Nvidia to reinstate ‘brilliant’ Jensen Huang
articles.summary: US president calls tech giant to give former CEO ‘a second chance’ and urges him to ‘make a big apology’.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s founder stepped down over a scandal involving extramarital affairs.

“You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.”

Trump also described Jensen Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions”.

“I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back, because he created something with Blackwell,” Trump said, referring to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

Huang resigned on November 12, following media reports of an intimate relationship with an alleged spy for Beijing who may have helped route restricted chips to China. US intelligence officials are said to have previously known about the possible espionage link.

Two more affairs have since been reported. The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China’s defence industry through her family and associates.

Trump also appeared to contradict Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had said earlier on Friday that Jensen Huang did not come up in talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

“I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man,'” said Trump of his meeting with the Chinese president.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang offered to return to the company.

However, Nvidia’s board has ruled out his comeback. Board chairperson Harvey Jones said on an earnings call later that day that the directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and do not plan to reinstate him.

The scandal has also drawn in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas told The Wall Street Journal that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal broke, though he stopped short of calling for the commerce secretary’s resignation.

“I have not lost confidence,” Trump said, calling Lutnick “a different kind of a guy, very good businessman”.

Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January, are investigating whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm run by his sons, avoid losses tied to scrutiny of Nvidia’s links to a Chinese company.

articles.title: Psychology says people who avoid writing on the first page of a new notebook may find it difficult to disturb something that looks perfect
articles.summary: You buy a new notebook, open it and admire the clean white pages.
articles.body: You buy a new notebook, open it and admire the clean white pages. You may already have plans for it: writing down daily thoughts, making to-do lists, keeping a journal or recording ideas. But when it is time to begin, you hesitate.The first page seems too clean to write on. You consider starting from the second page instead. Perhaps you tell yourself that you will use the first page for something important later. Sometimes, you even leave the notebook untouched for days because you cannot decide what deserves to go on that opening page.It is an oddly familiar habit. You bought the notebook to write in it, yet the moment it is ready to be used, you do not want to spoil its untouched appearance. Psychology offers a few possible explanations for this behaviour, particularly through research on perfectionism, fear of making mistakes and the way people respond to new beginnings.Why does the first page feel more difficult to use than the rest?One reason may be the expectation that the first page should be special. Unlike the pages that follow, it represents the beginning of something. You might feel that the first entry should be meaningful, the handwriting should look neat and the layout should be organised.This creates a small but noticeable pressure. Instead of simply writing something, you start thinking about whether it is good enough to deserve a place in a brand-new notebook.The same person may have no problem filling the middle pages with shopping lists, rough notes and unfinished thoughts. But the first page feels different because it is the first visible mark on something that still looks perfect. This can be connected to perfectionism, particularly the concern over making mistakes.A 1993 study examined the relationship between different dimensions of perfectionism and irrational fears. The researchers studied 189 university students and found that self-oriented perfectionism and socially prescribed perfectionism were associated with fears of failure, making mistakes, losing control and looking foolish.Although the study did not investigate notebook use, it helps explain why some people may feel uncomfortable making the first visible mistake on something they want to keep neat. For someone who places high expectations on their own work, even a slightly uneven line or an imperfect heading may feel disappointing.The appeal of keeping something untouchedA new notebook represents possibility. Its blank pages can be used for almost anything, and none of those possibilities has been ruled out yet. Once you begin writing, however, the notebook starts taking a particular shape. The first page is no longer blank, your handwriting may not look exactly as you imagined, and the notebook begins to look used rather than new.For some people, delaying that first entry may be a way of holding on to the feeling that everything is still possible. There is a related idea in psychology called the *fresh-start effect*. It describes how people often feel more motivated to pursue goals when they encounter a new beginning.In a 2014 study , researchers examined how temporal landmarks influence people's motivation to pursue goals. Across three studies, they found that activities such as gym visits, online searches for dieting information and commitments to personal goals increased after landmarks such as the beginning of a new week, month or year.The researchers suggested that these moments help people mentally separate their present selves from past imperfections, making it easier to approach goals with a renewed sense of motivation. A new notebook can carry a similar feeling of possibility, although the study did not examine notebooks specifically.When wanting it perfect gets in the way of using itThe reluctance to write on the first page does not necessarily mean someone is a perfectionist. Some people simply like keeping new possessions clean, while others prefer starting their notes on a page that feels less important.But when the hesitation comes from worrying about messy handwriting, choosing the wrong words or making an irreversible mistake, the desire to keep something perfect can get in the way of its actual purpose.The same pattern can appear in other situations. Someone may hesitate to use a new set of expensive paints, wear a new pair of shoes or open a fresh packet of stationery because they do not want the items to lose their original condition.Sometimes, the hardest part of using a new notebook is accepting that it will never look untouched again.You use AI every day. articles.title: Who is Jordan Lane? Meet the former New South Wales MP who proposed to his girlfriend during his final speech to Parliament, leaving lawmakers cheering
articles.summary: What comes to mind when you think about a farewell speech?
articles.body: What comes to mind when you think about a farewell speech? A farewell speech in parliament usually feels a bit formulaic: lots of nods to colleagues, flashes of nostalgia, maybe some final words for the constituents back home.But when Jordan Lane stood for his last time in the New South Wales Legislative Assembly, he made it personal, and the ripple was electric!What happened?Per BBC News, in a moment that no one saw coming, Lane broke with all political tradition: he pulled out an engagement ring, turned to his longtime girlfriend Natalie sitting up in the public gallery, and popped the question right there in the chamber. “Speaker, my final question as the member for Ryde is for my great love, Natalie. Will you marry me?” The room exploded in applause, cheers, and probably a few teary eyes for good measure. Natalie said yes, of course. How could she not? Lane slipped the ring onto her finger, leaned in for a kiss, and made sure the historic moment would never be left out of the record. “I’d like to note for Hansard that she said ‘yes’,” he added, grinning.This wasn’t some spur-of-the-moment stunt. The now-viral proposal came during Lane’s official farewell on November 19, 2026, just after he’d revealed he wouldn’t run for re-election the following March. At only 32, Lane’s time in NSW politics was relatively brief, making his exit, and his proposal, feel all the more significant. It was a plot twist worthy of its own news cycle. Now, after the one-of-a-kind proposal, videos of the moment are spread across the Internet, adding a romantic exclamation mark to an otherwise standard political departure.Who is Jordan Lane?The man behind the viral proposal and that “yes” heard around New South Wales is a Liberal Party politician who’s represented Ryde, his hometown patch in northern Sydney, in the state parliament. Per News.com.au, he never strayed far from his roots: he was raised in Ryde, started as a City of Ryde councillor in 2017, and quickly built a reputation for digging into community issues and local government work.By 27, he was Ryde’s youngest mayor, officially running the show for a whirlwind year in 2022. He came into state politics amid tough competition, just barely defeating his Labor challenger by a mere 50 votes, which was a result so tight it triggered a recount, which grew his lead to 54 votes. He entered the NSW Parliament on March 25, 2023, with a reputation for working hard and always wearing his community on his sleeve.Lane’s time as a state MP was short but eventful. Ryde is something of a political swing seat, fiercely contested every election. As a newbie on the opposition benches, Lane had to adapt fast, balancing party expectations with the ever-shifting mood of local voters.Why is Jordan Lane leaving politics?Well, Lane’s decision to trade politics for a quieter life surprised many. On November 6, he let everyone know he wouldn’t return for a second term in the 2027 state poll, citing the personal and professional toll of public life. The timing was notable, as the NSW Liberal Party was already watching several senior members announce their own departures before the upcoming election, creating a sense of change in the party’s ranks. During his departing speech, Lane talked honestly about the sacrifices he, and anyone in public service, makes.But at the heart of his words was something deeper: “Today I’m taking a big step,” he said, clearly shifting from the political to the personal. “In my heart I know this step is right because what underpins it is a value that I’ve literally worn on my chest for years — love.” He spun that thread through to his proposal, linking the unpredictability and passion of love to the wild, unpredictable game of politics.Who is Natalie, Jordan Lane's longtime girlfriend?Although Lane’s proposal was the highlight in the parliament, the real scene-stealer was Natalie Hissey, Lane’s girlfriend of more than a decade. She has been by his side since their chance meeting in their early twenties, and by all accounts, she had no inkling a marriage proposal was coming that day in parliament.After Lane’s speech, Natalie described it as “very meaningful” and, judging by the reactions and the way the story spread, a lot of others agreed. This wasn’t just another couple getting engaged; it was the closing of one defining chapter and the first page of another. Lane and Hissey’s story gave a human touch to a place better known for policy debates than grand gestures of the heart.Even the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, Greg Piper, couldn’t resist a joke, dubbing the 58th Parliament the “parliament of love.” Lane’s final question as Ryde’s member squeaked in just under the official wire — not about bills, alliances, or political records, but about the future he and Natalie would share. And as he made sure to have entered into Hansard, the answer was a resounding yes!You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: Former Jackson, Mississippi, mayor sentenced to more than 3 years for bribery scheme
articles.summary: The former mayor of Mississippi’s capital city was sentenced Friday to more than three years in prison after pleading guilty in a bribery scheme that included several other high-ranking Democratic county and city officials.
articles.body: JACKSON, Miss. — The former mayor of Mississippi’s capital city was sentenced Friday to more than three years in prison after pleading guilty in a bribery scheme that included several other high-ranking Democratic county and city officials. Former Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba was charged after two people working for the FBI posed as real estate developers and provided payments to officials, including $50,000 for Lumumba’s reelection campaign, in exchange for assistance greenlighting a development project, according to a 2024 indictment. In addition to his prison sentence, Lumumba will also forfeit $50,000 of property and is subject to one year of supervised release. Lumumba was charged alongside former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens and former Jackson City Council President Aaron Banks. Owens, who was charged on accusations that he solicited $250,000 in bribes, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to more than three years in prison earlier this month. Banks also pleaded guilty and was sentenced to nearly four years in prison. Former Jackson City Council Vice President Angelique Lee and Sherik Marve Smith, a businessman and relative of Owens, pleaded guilty to federal bribery charges in 2024. Lumumba, who served two terms as mayor, lost his reelection bid in 2025, shortly after he was charged in the scheme. The son of human rights activist and attorney Chokwe Lumumba, who died shortly after being elected Jackson mayor in 2013, the younger Lumumba began his career as an activist. Lumumba was first elected in 2017 and presided over the city during a water crisis that drew national attention. Lumumba’s lawyers did not immediately return an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on his sentencing.
